intro: STL to GLB converts 3D models from STL to GLB on the server, with nothing to install. It is useful, for example, to show a part on a website, in a catalogue or in augmented reality without installing anything. GLB is the binary version of glTF, the web's 3D format: browsers, the Windows 3D viewer, Android augmented reality and editors such as Blender show it, always in metres and with the Y axis up.

STL is the format every slicer reads (PrusaSlicer, Cura, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer): it only stores triangles, with no units or colours. As glTF uses metres and the Y axis up, the model is converted to metres and turned so it stands upright in viewers; the advanced options let you keep the axes.

You can apply a scale, choose the original's units if the STL does not store them and decide what to do with the parts: keep them separate inside the GLB when the format allows it, merge them into one mesh or get one file per part in a ZIP.

The STL geometry reaches the GLB without being simplified or repaired. Up to one million triangles are accepted without an account, two million with a free account and ten million with Pro, and up to ten files per task; they are processed on our server in the European Union and deleted when they expire.
steps: Upload one or more STL files.
Choose the units and, optionally, the scale and parts.

faq.q: Why does the GLB come out rotated or on its side?
faq.a: Because STL and GLB may use different axes. Try ticking or unticking “Keep the original axes” in the advanced options.
The STL material colours go into the GLB if the format supports them; STL stores no colours and the note says so.

faq.q: What if the model has holes?
faq.a: The GLB has the same geometry as the STL. To close them before printing, use Repair STL.
